title: The end of an era for China's economy
gist: Zhu Rongji's death prompts Noah Smith to argue that the catch-up growth formula Zhu built (SOE privatization, WTO entry, tax reform) is exhausted, with official Chinese GDP growth down to 5% (maybe 2-3% by independent estimates), leaving China with a k-shaped economy split between a world-class high-tech manufacturing sector and a broader economy still scarred by the real-estate bust, while it remains unclear whether Xi's industrial-subsidy push can replace catch-up growth with frontier innovation.

insights.claim: Zhu Rongji, who presided over China's economic policy from 1991 to 2003, drove the privatization of state-owned enterprises, championed China's WTO accession, deregulated to attract foreign manufacturing investment, bailed out China's banks after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and devised a major tax reform that shifted local government revenue to the central government while letting localities borrow more and sell more land leases.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Zhu's central-local fiscal split (more central revenue, more local land-lease and borrowing power) is the origin of the local-government land-finance model now unwinding in China's real estate bust.
insights.quote: Zhu Rongji's formula won't work anymore. But that doesn't mean Xi Jinping's will work either.
insights.locator: The end of an era for China's economy

insights.claim: When Zhu Rongji took office, East Asia had 1.22 billion people living on less than $3 a day (in 2021 dollars), more than half the world's total in poverty; by the time Xi Jinping became China's top leader, that number was down to one-sixth of what it had been.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the scale of what's now ending: the fastest large-scale poverty reduction in human history was built on a specific reform playbook that no longer applies at China's current income level.
insights.quote: This is the biggest and fastest decrease in absolute poverty that the human race has ever seen.
insights.locator: There is no question in my mind

insights.claim: Noah Smith regards Zhu Rongji as one of history's great heroes, arguing few individuals besides Deng Xiaoping have done more to reduce aggregate human suffering.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sets the normative benchmark Smith uses to judge whether Xi's current model can match Zhu's results.
insights.quote: There is no question in my mind that Zhu ought to be remembered as one of history’s great heroes.
insights.locator: There is no question in my mind

themes.theme: China's growth slowdown and data uncertainty

insights.claim: Over the last 15 years China's official growth rate has fallen to about 5%, less than half of what it was during Zhu Rongji's tenure, and some independent estimates put current growth as low as 2-3%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A sub-3% real growth rate would materially change assumptions embedded in China-linked equities, commodity demand forecasts, and global growth models that still price in higher official figures.
insights.quote: China’s growth rate has fallen to 5% — less than half of what it was in Zhu’s time
insights.locator: China is no longer the growth powerhouse

insights.claim: Chinese leaders have a tradition of 'smoothing' official growth statistics by understating growth during booms and overstating it during busts, so official figures likely understate the current slowdown's severity less than a naive reading would suggest.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investors relying on headline Chinese GDP prints should discount them and weight independent estimates (2-3% range) more heavily when sizing China exposure.
insights.quote: its leaders have a tradition of “smoothing” official numbers by understating growth during booms and overstating it during busts
insights.locator: Some independent estimates put the growth rate

insights.claim: China is now roughly five times richer than when Zhu left office in 2003, when it was about as rich as Tanzania or Zambia; today it is closer in per-capita terms to Argentina or the Dominican Republic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: China has graduated out of the income band where catch-up growth mechanically works, explaining why the old playbook of export-led, investment-heavy growth can't be repeated at the same pace.
insights.quote: When Zhu ended his historic tenure in 2003, China was about as rich as Tanzania or Zambia is now. Today, it’s closer to Argentina or the Dominican Republic.
insights.locator: China is a much richer country

insights.claim: There is an active debate over whether Chinese total factor productivity actually grew during the 2010s: the Penn World Tables recently revised their methodology and now show healthy annualized TFP growth of over 2%, while the Conference Board and Brandt et al. (2022) still peg TFP growth at around 1%, but all sources agree TFP growth has been slowing over time and Xi's industrial policy hasn't managed to re-accelerate it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Whether China's efficiency gains are real or a data-revision artifact is a live methodological fight that should make investors skeptical of any single TFP series used to underwrite China growth theses.
insights.quote: everyone agrees that China’s TFP growth has been slowing over time, and that Xi’s “industrial policy for everything” hasn’t managed to re-accelerate it so far

themes.theme: Xi's industrial-policy pivot and the two-speed economy

insights.claim: Xi Jinping has built a 'new national system' coordinating the entire innovation supply chain from state research labs to private product companies, alongside the most extensive system of industrial subsidies in world history covering nearly every advanced manufacturing industry plus AI, aimed at pushing China past middle-income status via frontier innovation rather than catch-up growth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals continued heavy state capital allocation into Chinese advanced manufacturing and AI regardless of near-term growth pain, a structural tailwind for related Chinese industrial-policy sectors even as broader growth slows.
insights.quote: He has unleashed the most expensive and extensive system of industrial subsidies in world history, promoting essentially every advanced manufacturing industry in existence, as well as AI.

insights.claim: China now appears to have a 'two-speed' or 'k-shaped' economy, split between a high-tech manufacturing sector that is increasingly the envy of the world and a broader economy still mired in the aftermath of the country's real estate bust.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investors should differentiate exposure: advanced-manufacturing/export champions may keep outperforming even as domestic-demand, property, and consumer-linked sectors remain structurally depressed.
insights.quote: China now appears to have a “two-speed” or “k-shaped” economy — split between a high-tech manufacturing sector that’s increasingly the envy of the world, and a broader economy that’s still mired
insights.locator: a lot of people are noting

insights.claim: It remains unclear whether Xi's industrial-policy model can actually replace the catch-up growth model Zhu Rongji built, even though its stated goal of pushing China toward frontier innovation is the right one.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the central open question for China-watchers: whether current subsidy-driven industrial policy can substitute for the exhausted Zhu-era reform-and-opening growth engine.
insights.quote: Whether Xi’s policies have been effective at this goal is less clear.
insights.locator: Whether Xi's policies have been effective
